{{short description|Percent of variation in IQ scores in a given population associated with genetic variation}}
Research on the [[heritability]] of [[intelligence quotient]] (IQ) inquires into the degree of variation in IQ within a [[Population (human biology)|population]] that is associated with [[genetic variation]] between individuals in that population. There has been significant controversy in the academic community about the '''heritability of IQ''' since research on the issue began in the late nineteenth century.<ref name="devlin">{{cite journal |last1=Devlin |first1=B. |last2=Daniels |first2=Michael |last3=Roeder |first3=Kathryn |author3-link=Kathryn Roeder |year=1997 |title=The heritability of IQ |journal=Nature |volume=388 |issue=6641 |pages=468–71 |bibcode=1997Natur.388..468D |doi=10.1038/41319 |pmid=9242404 |s2cid=4313884 |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name="rose">{{cite journal |last1=Rose |first1=Steven P R |date=June 2006 |title=Commentary: Heritability estimates—long past their sell-by date |journal=International Journal of Epidemiology |volume=35 |issue=3 |pages=525–527 |doi=10.1093/ije/dyl064 |pmid=16645027 |doi-access=free}}</ref> [[Intelligence]] in the normal range is a [[Quantitative trait locus#Quantitative traits|polygenic trait]], meaning that it is influenced by more than one gene,<ref>Alice Marcus. 2010. Human Genetics: An Overview. Alpha Science section 14.5</ref><ref name=Davies2011>{{cite journal | last1 = Davies | first1 = G. | last2 = Tenesa | first2 = A. | last3 = Payton | first3 = A. | last4 = Yang | first4 = J. | last5 = Harris | first5 = S. E. | last6 = Liewald | first6 = D. | last7 = Deary | first7 = I. J. | year = 2011 | title = Genome-wide association studies establish that human intelligence is highly heritable and polygenic | journal = Molecular Psychiatry | volume = 16 | issue = 10| pages = 996–1005 | doi = 10.1038/mp.2011.85 | pmid=21826061 | pmc=3182557}}</ref> and in the case of intelligence at least 500 genes.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.newscientist.com/article/2163484-found-more-than-500-genes-that-are-linked-to-intelligence/|title=Found: more than 500 genes that are linked to intelligence|first=New Scientist staff and Press|last=Association|website=New Scientist|access-date=2018-11-29|archive-date=2019-12-13|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191213201937/https://www.newscientist.com/article/2163484-found-more-than-500-genes-that-are-linked-to-intelligence/|url-status=live}}</ref> Further, explaining the similarity in IQ of closely related persons requires careful study because environmental factors may be correlated with genetic factors. Outside the normal range, certain single gene [[genetic disorder]]s, such as [[phenylketonuria]], can negatively affect intelligence.<ref name="general">{{cite book |author1=Robert J. Sternberg |url=https://archive.org/details/generalfactorint00ster_484 |title=The general factor of intelligence |author2=Elena Grigorenko |publisher=Lawrence Erlbaum Associates |year=2002 |isbn=978-0-8058-3675-2 |pages=[https://archive.org/details/generalfactorint00ster_484/page/n272 260]–261 |url-access=limited}}{{page needed|date=April 2013}}</ref>

Estimates in the academic research of the heritability of IQ vary significantly by study and by study design. The general figure for heritability of IQ from behavioral genetic studies is about 0.5 across multiple studies in varying populations.<ref name=":4">{{cite book |last1=Plomin |first1=Robert |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=OytMMAEACAAJ |title=Behavioral Genetics |last2=DeFries |first2=John C. |last3=Knopik |first3=Valerie S. |last4=Neiderhiser |first4=Jenae M. |date=24 September 2012 |publisher=Worth Publishers |isbn=978-1-4292-4215-8 |pages=195–196 |quote= |access-date=4 September 2013}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=172}} The relationship between heritability and age is uncertain, though most researchers believe that there is an increase in heritability over the course of the lifespan and that this increase reflects the importance of gene-environment correlations. Recent genetic research has come to more equivocal results, with estimates of heritability lower than those derived from twin studies, causing what is known as the "[[missing heritability problem]]".

Although IQ differences between individuals have been shown to have a hereditary component, it does not follow that disparities in IQ between groups have a genetic basis.<ref name=":10">{{Cite journal == Heritability and caveats ==
{{Main|Heritability}}

Heritability is a [[statistic]] used in the fields of [[Animal husbandry|breeding]] and [[genetics]] that estimates the degree of ''variation'' in a [[phenotypic trait]] in a population is explained by genetic variation between individuals in that population.<ref name="scitable-estimating">{{cite journal |last1=Wray |first1=Naomi |last2=Visscher |first2=Peter |name-list-style=vanc |date=2008 |title=Estimating Trait Heritability |url=http://www.nature.com/scitable/topicpage/estimating-trait-heritability-46889 |url-status=live |journal=Nature Education |volume=1 |issue=1 |page=29 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150802043009/http://www.nature.com/scitable/topicpage/estimating-trait-heritability-46889 |archive-date=2 August 2015 |access-date=24 July 2015}}</ref> The concept of heritability can be expressed in the form of the following question: "What is the proportion of the variation in a given trait within a population that is ''not'' explained by the environment or random chance?"<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gazzaniga |first1=Michael S |title=Psychological science |last2=Heatherton |first2=Todd F |last3=Halpern |first3=Diane F |date=February 2015 |isbn=978-0-393-26313-8 |edition=5th |location=New York |publisher=W.W. Norton |oclc=908409996 |name-list-style=vanc}}</ref>

Estimates of heritability take values ranging from 0 to 1; a heritability estimate of 1 indicates that all variation in the trait in question is genetic and a heritability estimate of 0 indicates that ''none'' of the variation is genetic.

There are a number of caveats to consider when interpreting heritability:
* Heritability measures the proportion of ''variation'' in a trait that can be attributed to genes, and not the proportion of a trait caused by genes.<ref name=":40">{{Cite journal |last1=Moore |first1=David S. |author-link1=David Moore (psychologist)|last2=Shenk |first2=David |date=2017 |title=The heritability fallacy |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/wcs.1400 |journal=WIREs Cognitive Science |language=en |volume=8 |issue=1–2 |article-number=e1400 |doi=10.1002/wcs.1400 |pmid=27906501 |issn=1939-5086|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Thus, if the environment relevant to a given trait changes in a way that affects all members of the population equally, the mean value of the trait will change without any change in its heritability (because the variation or differences among individuals in the population will stay the same). This has evidently happened for height: the heritability of stature is high, but average heights continue to increase.<ref name="unknown">{{cite journal |doi=10.1037/0003-066X.51.2.77 |title=Intelligence: Knowns and unknowns |year=1996 |last1=Neisser |first1=Ulric |last2=Boodoo |first2=Gwyneth |last3=Bouchard |first3=Thomas J. Jr. |last4=Boykin |first4=A. Wade |last5=Brody |first5=Nathan |last6=Ceci |first6=Stephen J. |last7=Halpern |first7=Diane F. |last8=Loehlin |first8=John C. |last9=Perloff |first9=Robert |last10=Sternberg |first10=Robert J. |last11=Urbina |first11=Susana |journal=American Psychologist |volume=51 |issue=2 |pages=77–101|display-authors=8 |bibcode=1996AmPsy..51...77N }}</ref> Thus, even in developed nations, a high heritability of a trait does not necessarily mean that average group differences are due to genes.<ref name="unknown"/><ref>{{cite journal |first1=Jeanne |last1=Brooks-Gunn |first2=Pamela K. |last2=Klebanov |first3=Greg J. |last3=Duncan |year=1996 |title=Ethnic Differences in Children's Intelligence Test Scores: Role of Economic Deprivation, Home Environment, and Maternal Characteristics |journal=Child Development |volume=67 |issue=2 |pages=396–408 |jstor=1131822 |doi=10.2307/1131822 |pmid=8625720}}</ref> Some have gone further, and used height as an example in order to argue that "even highly heritable traits can be strongly manipulated by the environment, so heritability has little if anything to do with controllability."<ref name="JohnsonBouchard2009">{{cite journal |doi=10.1111/j.1467-8721.2009.01639.x |title=Beyond Heritability: Twin Studies in Behavioral Research |year=2009 |last1=Johnson |first1=Wendy |last2=Turkheimer |first2=Eric |last3=Gottesman |first3=Irving I. |last4=Bouchard Jr. |first4=Thomas J. |journal=Current Directions in Psychological Science |volume=18 |issue=4 |pages=217–20 |pmid=20625474 |pmc=2899491}}</ref>
* A common error is to assume that a heritability figure is necessarily unchangeable. The value of heritability can change if the impact of environment (or of genes) in the population is substantially altered.<ref name="unknown"/> If the environmental variation encountered by different individuals increases, then the heritability figure would decrease. On the other hand, if everyone had the same environment, then heritability would be 100%. The population in developing nations often has more diverse environments than in developed nations. This would mean that heritability figures would be lower in developing nations. Another example is [[phenylketonuria]] which previously caused [[Intellectual disability|intellectual disabilities]] in everyone who had this genetic disorder and thus had a heritability of 100%. Today, this can be prevented by following a modified diet, resulting in a lowered heritability.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Haworth |first1=Claire |last2=Davis |first2=Oliver |date=2014 |title=From observational to dynamic genetics |journal=Frontiers in Genetics |volume=5 |page=6 |doi=10.3389/fgene.2014.00006 |issn=1664-8021 |pmc=3896969 |pmid=24478793 |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* A high heritability of a trait does not mean that  effects such as learning are not involved. Vocabulary size, for example, is substantially heritable (and highly correlated with general intelligence) although every word in an individual's vocabulary is learned. In a society in which plenty of words are available in everyone's environment, especially for individuals who are motivated to seek them out, the number of words that individuals actually learn depends to a considerable extent on their genetic predispositions and thus heritability is high.<ref name="unknown"/>
* Contrary to popular belief, two parents of higher IQ will not necessarily produce offspring of equal or higher intelligence. Polygenic traits often appear less heritable at the extremes. A heritable trait is definitionally more likely to appear in the offspring of two parents high in that trait than in the offspring of two randomly selected parents. However, the more extreme the expression of the trait in the parents, the less likely the child is to display the same extreme as the parents. In fact, parents whose IQ is at either extreme are more likely to produce offspring with IQ closer to the mean (or average) than they are to produce offspring with high IQ. At the same time, the more extreme the expression of the trait in the parents, the more likely the child is to express the trait at all. For example, the child of two extremely tall parents is likely to be taller than the average person (displaying the trait), but unlikely to be taller than the two parents (displaying the trait at the same extreme). See also [[regression toward the mean]].<ref name="HMG4">{{cite book|last1=Strachan|first1=Tom|last2=Read|first2=Andrew|title=Human Molecular Genetics, Fourth Edition|url=https://archive.org/details/humanmolecularge00stra_254|url-access=limited|publisher=Garland Science|location=New York| year=2011|isbn=978-0-8153-4149-9|pages=[https://archive.org/details/humanmolecularge00stra_254/page/n93 80]–81}}</ref><ref name="Humphreys1978">{{cite journal |last1=Humphreys |first1=Lloyd G. |title=To understand regression from parent to offspring, think statistically |journal=Psychological Bulletin |date=1978 |volume=85 |issue=6 |pages=1317–1322 |doi=10.1037/0033-2909.85.6.1317 |pmid=734015 }}</ref><ref>Schacter, Daniel, Daniel Gilbert, and Daniel Wegner. "Intelligence." Psychology. 2 ed. New York: Worth Publishers, 2010. 405-406. Print.</ref>

== Methodology ==
{{See also|Behavioural genetics|Quantitative genetics}}
There are multiple types of studies that are designed to estimate heritability and other variance components, stemming from the field of [[Biometrics|biometrical]] genetics.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Evans |first1=David M. |last2=Gillespie |first2=N. A. |last3=Martin |first3=N. G. |date=2002-10-01 |title=Biometrical genetics |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0301051102000510 |journal=Biological Psychology |volume=61 |issue=1 |pages=33–51 |doi=10.1016/S0301-0511(02)00051-0 |pmid=12385668 |issn=0301-0511|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The [[variance]], or more simply the differences in a trait within a population, can be partitioned into specific variance components that are based on particular decomposition models for the [[phenotype]]. First pointed out by [[Ronald Fisher]] and [[Sewall Wright]], different sources of variance differ in their contribution to the resemblance between types of relatives.<ref name=":11">{{Cite book |last=Lynch |first=Michael |title=Genetics and Analysis of Quantitative Traits |publisher=Sinauer Associates |year=1998 |isbn=978-0-87893-481-2}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=131}}By making certain assumptions about the relationship between genes and environment, the field of [[quantitative genetics]] has developed equations that describe the expected correlation between relatives in terms of specific variance components (shared environment, additive genetic, etc.).<ref name=":11" />{{Reference page|pages=163-167}}
[[File:Graham Coop textbook diagram.png|thumb|Correlation between relatives on a purely additive genetic model of phenotypic determination, from Coop 2020<ref>{{Cite book |last=Coop |first=Graham |url=https://github.com/cooplab/popgen-notes/releases/tag/v1.2 |title=Population and Quantitative Genetics |date=21 September 2020 |edition=3rd}}</ref>]]
One simple case is presented by twin studies. By making assumptions about genetic additivity and sources of environmental variation, researchers can estimate the heritability of a phenotype by comparing the resemblance of twins.<ref name=":11" />{{Reference page|page=581}} Another method used to estimate heritability is adoption studies. Because adoptive parents and their adoptive children share a common environment, but not genetics,<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|pages=80-82}} researchers in behavioral genetics have used data from adoptive families to estimate the heritability of IQ.<ref name=":16">{{Cite journal |last1=Richardson |first1=Ken |last2=Norgate |first2=Sarah H. |date=2006 |title=A Critical Analysis of IQ Studies of Adopted Children |url=https://karger.com/article/doi/10.1159/000096531 |journal=Human Development |language=en |volume=49 |issue=6 |pages=319–335 |doi=10.1159/000096531 |issn=0018-716X}}</ref><ref name=":15" /> Based on quantitative genetic theory, some researchers have taken a broader approach to analyzing familial resemblance. These researchers typically use [[Path analysis (statistics)|path analysis]]{{Efn|For the full series of papers developing the method, see <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rice |first1=J. |last2=Cloninger |first2=C. R. |last3=Reich |first3=T. |date=November 1978 |title=Multifactorial inheritance with cultural transmission and assortative mating. I. Description and basic properties of the unitary models |journal=American Journal of Human Genetics |volume=30 |issue=6 |pages=618–643 |issn=0002-9297 |pmc=1685878 |pmid=747189}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cloninger |first1=C. R. |last2=Rice |first2=J. |last3=Reich |first3=T. |date=March 1979 |title=Multifactorial inheritance with cultural transmission and assortative mating. II. a general model of combined polygenic and cultural inheritance |journal=American Journal of Human Genetics |volume=31 |issue=2 |pages=176–198 |issn=0002-9297 |pmc=1685756 |pmid=453202}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cloninger |first1=C. R. |last2=Rice |first2=J. |last3=Reich |first3=T. |date=May 1979 |title=Multifactorial inheritance with cultural transmission and assortative mating. III. Family structure and the analysis of separation experiments |journal=American Journal of Human Genetics |volume=31 |issue=3 |pages=366–388 |issn=0002-9297 |pmc=1685778 |pmid=572636}}</ref>}} to fit models using larger sets of familiar correlations, incorporating cultural transmission, adoption, other complex living arrangements, and generalized assortative mating.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rao |first1=D. C. |last2=Morton |first2=N. E. |last3=Cloninger |first3=C. R. |date=April 1979 |title=Path analysis under generalized assortative mating: I. Theory |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/genetics-research/article/path-analysis-under-generalized-assortative-mating/F1784B9BD698D00E3D202CD61066C8B0 |journal=Genetics Research |language=en |volume=33 |issue=2 |pages=175–188 |doi=10.1017/S0016672300018310 |pmid=478296 |issn=1469-5073}}</ref><ref name=":14">{{Cite journal |last1=Feldman |first1=Marcus W. |last2=Ramachandran |first2=Sohini |date=2018-02-12 |title=Missing compared to what? Revisiting heritability, genes and culture |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |volume=373 |issue=1743 |article-number=20170064 |doi=10.1098/rstb.2017.0064 |pmc=5812976 |pmid=29440529}}</ref> However, with the transition into the [[postgenomic era]], issues with controversial assumptions in previous models analyzing familial resemblance may be superseded by genetic analysis.<ref name=":10" /> Methods have developed in genetic analysis to estimate the total heritability of a trait using large datasets with millions of genetic variants.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Zaitlen |first1=Noah |last2=Kraft |first2=Peter |date=2012-10-01 |title=Heritability in the genome-wide association era |journal=Human Genetics |language=en |volume=131 |issue=10 |pages=1655–1664 |doi=10.1007/s00439-012-1199-6 |issn=1432-1203 |pmc=3432754 |pmid=22821350}}</ref><ref name=":20">{{Cite journal |last1=Tang |first1=Mingsheng |last2=Wang |first2=Tong |last3=Zhang |first3=Xuefen |date=2022-03-14 |title=A review of SNP heritability estimation methods |url=https://academic.oup.com/bib/article/23/3/bbac067/6548385 |journal=Briefings in Bioinformatics |language=en |volume=23 |issue=3 |article-number=bbac067 |doi=10.1093/bib/bbac067 |pmid=35289357 |issn=1467-5463 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250826140022/https://academic.oup.com/bib/article/23/3/bbac067/6548385 |archive-date=2025-08-26 |access-date=2025-10-14 |url-status=live |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

In the case of IQ, heritability estimates based on direct observation of molecular genetics have been significantly lower (around 10%) than those employing traditional methods (40–80%).<ref name=":13" /><ref name=":12" /> This discrepancy has been termed the "missing heritability problem."<ref name=":13" /> While researchers such as [[Robert Plomin]] and [[Sophie von Stumm]] contend that this gap will likely disappear with the acquisition of more genetic data, [[Eric Turkheimer]] and Lucas J. Matthews argue that it reveals a deeper set of methodological problem inherent in the concept of heritability itself, which will not be easy to overcome.<ref name=":13" />

== Estimates ==
Although individual family studies that estimate the heritability of IQ vary greatly,{{Efn|For example, individual studies have estimated values as low as "not significantly different from zero" <ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Adams |first1=B. |last2=Ghodsian |first2=M. |last3=Richardson |first3=K. |date=September 1976 |title=Evidence for a low upper limit of heritability of mental test performance in a national sample of twins |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/263314a0 |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=263 |issue=5575 |pages=314–316 |doi=10.1038/263314a0 |pmid=986563 |bibcode=1976Natur.263..314A |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> to as high as over .8.}} most family studies estimate the heritability of IQ in the range from 0.4 to 0.8<ref name=":1" /> and reviews of the literature typically summarize classical family design research with an estimate of 0.5.<ref name=":13">{{Cite journal |last1=Matthews |first1=Lucas J. |last2=Turkheimer |first2=Eric |date=2022-06-01 |title=Three legs of the missing heritability problem |journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science |volume=93 |pages=183–191 |doi=10.1016/j.shpsa.2022.04.004 |pmid=35533541 |pmc=9172633 |issn=0039-3681}}</ref><ref name=":12">{{Cite journal |last1=Plomin |first1=Robert |last2=von Stumm |first2=Sophie |date=8 January 2018 |title=The new genetics of intelligence |journal=Nature Reviews. Genetics |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=148–159 |doi=10.1038/nrg.2017.104 |issn=1471-0064 |pmc=5985927 |pmid=29335645}}</ref> Issues with the methodology of family studies have long plagued the research field,<ref>{{Cite book |last=Panofsky |first=Aaron |title=Misbehaving Science: Controversy and the Development of Behavior Genetics |date=2014 |publisher=University of Chicago Press |isbn=978-0-226-05845-0 |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Meyer |first1=Michelle N |last2=Appelbaum |first2=Paul S. |last3=Benjamin |first3=Daniel J. |last4=Callier |first4=Shawneequa |last5=Comfort |first5=Nathaniel |last6=Conley |first6=Dalton |last7=Freese |first7=Jeremy |last8=Garrison |first8=Nanibaa' A |last9=Hammonds |first9=Evelyn M. |last10=Harden |first10=K. Paige |last11=Lee |first11=Sandra Soo-Jin |last12=Martin |first12=Alicia R. |last13=Martschenko |first13=Daphne Oluwaseun |last14=Neale |first14=Benjamin M. |last15=et. |first15=al |date=20 April 2023 |title=Wrestling with Social and Behavioral Genomics: Risks, Potential Benefits, and Ethical Responsibility |journal=The Hastings Center Report |volume=53 |issue=S1 |pages=S2–S49 |doi=10.1002/hast.1477 |pmid=37078667 |pmc=10433733 }}</ref> but some researchers now believe that genome-wide association studies can provide less biased estimates of heritability.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Jian |last2=Zeng |first2=Jian |last3=Goddard |first3=Michael E. |last4=Wray |first4=Naomi R. |last5=Visscher |first5=Peter M. |date=1 September 2017 |title=Concepts, estimation and interpretation of SNP-based heritability |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/ng.3941 |journal=Nature Genetics |language=en |volume=49 |issue=9 |pages=1304–1310 |doi=10.1038/ng.3941 |pmid=28854176 |issn=1546-1718|url-access=subscription }}</ref> These genomic studies provide estimates of heritability that are much lower than those derived from twin studies, leading to what is denoted as the "missing heritability problem".<ref name=":21">{{Cite journal |last=Young |first=Alexander I. |date=2019-06-24 |title=Solving the missing heritability problem |journal=PLOS Genetics |language=en |volume=15 |issue=6 |doi=10.1371/journal.pgen.1008222 |issn=1553-7404 |pmc=6611648 |pmid=31233496 |doi-access=free |article-number=e1008222}}</ref> The latest results from genomic methods are between 0.10 to 0.20,<ref name=":13" /> and researchers have proposed various theories to explain the gap.<ref name=":27" /><ref>{{Cite book |last1=Rizzi |first1=Thais S. |title=The Oxford handbook of cognitive psychology |last2=Posthuma |first2=Danielle |date=2013 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-997830-4 |editor-last=Reisberg |editor-first=Daniel |series=Oxford library of psychology |location=New York Oxford |pages=834–836 |chapter=Genes and Intelligence}}</ref>

=== Twin and family research ===
{{See also|Twin study|Adoption study}}

==== Twin studies ====
Twin studies are the most common method used to estimate the heritability of most traits.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Polderman |first1=Tinca J. C. |last2=Benyamin |first2=Beben |last3=de Leeuw |first3=Christiaan A. |last4=Sullivan |first4=Patrick F. |last5=van Bochoven |first5=Arjen |last6=Visscher |first6=Peter M. |last7=Posthuma |first7=Danielle |date=July 2015 |title=Meta-analysis of the heritability of human traits based on fifty years of twin studies |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/ng.3285 |journal=Nature Genetics |language=en |volume=47 |issue=7 |pages=702–709 |doi=10.1038/ng.3285 |pmid=25985137 |bibcode=2015NaGen..47..702P |issn=1546-1718}}</ref> Because [[monozygotic]] twins derive from one fertilized egg, they are largely genetically identical,{{Efn|Strictly speaking, monozygotic twins are not purely genetically identical due to somatic mosaicism and mutations.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Charney |first=Evan |date=2012-10-24 |title=Behavior genetics and postgenomics |url=https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/behavioral-and-brain-sciences/article/abs/behavior-genetics-and-postgenomics/AEDDF1A7D830480B80BF5A5BD7BD5BD0 |journal=Behavioral and Brain Sciences |language=en |volume=35 |issue=5 |pages=331–358 |doi=10.1017/S0140525X11002226 |pmid=23095378 |issn=0140-525X|url-access=subscription }}</ref>}} while [[dizygotic]] twins are expected to share 50% of their DNA.<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|pages=85-86}} Twin studies compare the resemblance of monozygotic twins to the resemblance of dizygotic twins to estimate the heritability of a trait using various models.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Verweij |first1=Karin J. H. |chapter=Estimating Heritability from Twin Studies |date=2012 |title=Statistical Human Genetics: Methods and Protocols |pages=151–170 |editor-last=Elston |editor-first=Robert C.  |place=Totowa, NJ |publisher=Humana Press |language=en |doi=10.1007/978-1-61779-555-8_9 |isbn=978-1-61779-555-8 |last2=Mosing |first2=Miriam A. |last3=Zietsch |first3=Brendan P. |last4=Medland |first4=Sarah E. |series=Methods in Molecular Biology |volume=850 |pmid=22307698 |editor2-last=Satagopan |editor2-first=Jaya M.|editor2-link=Jaya Satagopan |editor3-last=Sun |editor3-first=Shuying}}</ref>

Twin studies have shown greater resemblance between monozygotic twins than dizygotic twins.<ref name=":4" /> This has lead most researchers in behavioral genetics to conclude that the heritability of IQ is in a range between 0.4 to 0.8.<ref name=":1" />{{Reference page|page=132|quote=Most studies estimate that the heritability of IQ is somewhere between .4 and .8 (and generally less for children), but it really makes no sense to talk about a single value for the heritability of intelligence.}}<ref name=":19">{{Cite book |last=Ceci |first=Stephen |title=On Intelligence: A Biological Treatise on Intellectual Development |publisher=Harvard University Press |isbn=978-0-674-63456-5 |edition=1st |publication-date=1 September 1996}}</ref>{{Rp|page=143}} However, it is not clear if all of the assumptions in twin studies hold true.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Stenberg |first=Anders |date=2013-03-01 |title=Interpreting estimates of heritability – A note on the twin decomposition |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1570677X12000731 |journal=Economics & Human Biology |volume=11 |issue=2 |pages=201–205 |doi=10.1016/j.ehb.2012.05.002 |pmid=22676967 |issn=1570-677X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Critics often focus on the equal environment assumption, which is the assumption that environmentally caused similarity is the same for both monozygotic and dizygotic twins.<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|page=86}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Richardson |first1=Ken |last2=Norgate |first2=Sarah |date=2005 |title=The equal environments assumption of classical twin studies may not hold |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1348/000709904X24690 |journal=British Journal of Educational Psychology |language=en |volume=75 |issue=3 |pages=339–350 |doi=10.1348/000709904X24690 |pmid=16238870 |issn=2044-8279}}</ref> Genetic modeling has found that even in the complete absence of genetic factors for a trait, environmental similarity between monozygotic twins will cause heritability estimators to produce large estimates of genetic heritability.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Guo |first=Sun-Wei |date=1999 |title=The Behaviors of Some Heritability Estimators in the Complete Absence of Genetic Factors |url=https://karger.com/article/doi/10.1159/000022878 |journal=Human Heredity |language=en |volume=49 |issue=4 |pages=215–228 |doi=10.1159/000022878 |pmid=10436384 |issn=0001-5652|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Guo |first=Sun-Wei |date=2001 |title=Does Higher Concordance in Monozygotic Twins Than in Dizygotic Twins Suggest a Genetic Component? |url=https://karger.com/article/doi/10.1159/000053333 |journal=Human Heredity |language=en |volume=51 |issue=3 |pages=121–132 |doi=10.1159/000053333 |pmid=11173963 |issn=0001-5652|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Researchers have produced different analyses of the equal environment assumption,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Barnes |first1=J. C. |last2=Wright |first2=John Paul |last3=Boutwell |first3=Brian B. |last4=Schwartz |first4=Joseph A. |last5=Connolly |first5=Eric J. |last6=Nedelec |first6=Joseph L. |last7=Beaver |first7=Kevin M. |date=2014 |title=Demonstrating the Validity of Twin Research in Criminology |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1745-9125.12049 |journal=Criminology |language=en |volume=52 |issue=4 |pages=588–626 |doi=10.1111/1745-9125.12049 |issn=1745-9125|url-access=subscription }}</ref> some suggesting that the assumption is untenable for related traits like educational attainment.<ref>{{Cite report |url=https://liser.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/on-the-origins-of-socioeconomic-inequalities-evidence-from-twin-f |title=On the Origins of Socioeconomic Inequalities: Evidence from Twin Families |last1=Bingley |first1=Paul |last2=Cappellari |first2=Lorenzo |last3=Tatsiramos |first3=Konstantinos |date=5 Jul 2024 |issue=LISER Working Paper Series |access-date=13 October 2025 |url-status=live |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250708100608/https://liser.elsevierpure.com/en/publications/on-the-origins-of-socioeconomic-inequalities-evidence-from-twin-f |archive-date=8 July 2025}}</ref>

Twins reared apart have also been the subject of significant debate.<ref name=":17">{{Cite book |last=Bouchard |first=Thomas |title=Intelligence, heredity, and environment |date=1999 |publisher=Cambridge Univ. Press |isbn=978-0-521-46904-3 |editor-last=Sternberg |editor-first=Robert J. |edition=Repr |location=Cambridge |chapter=IQ similarity in twins reared apart: Findings and responses to critics}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Segal |first=Nancy L. |title=Deliberately Divided: Inside the Controversial Study of Twins and Triplets Adopted Apart |date=2021 |publisher=Rowman & Littlefield Publishing Group |isbn=978-1-5381-3285-2 |location= |language=en-US}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Joseph |first=Jay |url=https://www.taylorfrancis.com/books/9781317605911 |title=The Trouble with Twin Studies: A Reassessment of Twin Research in the Social and Behavioral Sciences |date=2014-11-20 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-315-74838-2 |edition=1 |language=en |doi=10.4324/9781315748382}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Farber |first=Susan L. |title=Identical twins reared apart: a reanalysis |date=1981 |publisher=Basic Books |isbn=978-0-465-03228-0 |location=New York}}</ref> The 2006 edition of ''Assessing adolescent and adult intelligence'' by [[Alan S. Kaufman]] and Elizabeth O. Lichtenberger reports correlations of 0.86 for identical twins raised together compared to 0.76 for those raised apart and 0.47 for siblings.<ref name="KaufmanLichtenberger2006">{{cite book |last1=Kaufman |first1=Alan S. |author-link1=Alan S. Kaufman |title=Assessing Adolescent and Adult Intelligence |last2=Lichtenberger |first2=Elizabeth |publisher=Wiley |year=2006 |isbn=978-0-471-73553-3 |edition=3rd |location=Hoboken (NJ)}}{{page needed|date=April 2013}}</ref> Theoretically, the correlation between twins reared apart is a direct estimate of heritability, as the only common factor between the twins would be the genetic variance.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pedersen |first1=N. L. |last2=Lichtenstein |first2=P. |last3=Plomin |first3=R. |last4=DeFaire |first4=U. |last5=McClearn |first5=G. E. |last6=Matthews |first6=K. A. |date=1989 |title=Genetic and environmental influences for type A-like measures and related traits: a study of twins reared apart and twins reared together |journal=Psychosomatic Medicine |volume=51 |issue=4 |pages=428–440 |doi=10.1097/00006842-198907000-00006 |issn=0033-3174 |pmid=2772107}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=431|quote=in the absence of correlated environments, the intraclass correlation for identical twins reared apart provides a direct estimate}} However, this makes an assumption of uncorrelated environments between twins, which may not be the case.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Joseph |first=Jay |date=2022 |title=A Reevaluation of the 1990 "Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart" IQ Study |url=https://karger.com/article/doi/10.1159/000521922 |journal=Human Development |language=en |volume=66 |issue=1 |pages=48–65 |doi=10.1159/000521922 |issn=0018-716X}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Nisbett |first=Richard E. |title=Intelligence and How to Get It: Why Schools and Cultures Count |title-link=Intelligence and How to Get It |publisher=W. W. Norton & Company |year=2009 |isbn=978-0-393-07141-2}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=26}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Kempthorne |first=Oscar |date=1978 |title=A Biometrics Invited Paper: Logical, Epistemological and Statistical Aspects of Nature-Nurture Data Interpretation |journal=Biometrics |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=1–23 |doi=10.2307/2529584 |jstor=2529584 |issn=0006-341X}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=18}} For example, some researchers argue that twins experience similar education and this causes increased similarity in IQ.<ref>{{Cite book |title=Making human beings human: bioecological perspectives on human development |date=2005 |publisher=Sage Publications |isbn=978-0-7619-2711-2 |editor-last=Bronfenbrenner |editor-first=Urie |series=The Sage program on applied developmental science |location=Thousand Oaks}}</ref>{{Reference page|pages=236-237}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Kamin |first=Leon |title=The Science and Politics of I.Q. |title-link=The Science and Politics of I.Q. |date=2012 |publisher=Taylor and Francis |isbn=978-0-89859-129-3 |location=Hoboken}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=67}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Horvath |first1=Jared C. |last2=Fabricant |first2=Katie |date=2025-07-01 |title=IQ differences of identical twins reared apart are significantly influenced by educational differences |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0001691825003853 |journal=Acta Psychologica |volume=257 |article-number=105072 |doi=10.1016/j.actpsy.2025.105072 |pmid=40403412 |issn=0001-6918|doi-access=free }}</ref> [[Thomas J. Bouchard Jr.|Thomas Bouchard]] argues that some previous analyses of the data on twins reared apart are an abuse of statistical theory that he calls "pseudoanalysis".<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bouchard |first=Thomas J. |date=March 1982 |title=Identical Twins Reared Apart: Reanalysis or Pseudo-analysis? |url=http://access.portico.org/stable?au=phzkfk9w1 |journal=Contemporary Psychology: A Journal of Reviews |volume=27 |issue=3 |pages=190–191 |doi=10.1037/021001|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":17" />{{Reference page|pages=146-147}}

==== Adoption studies ====
Another study design researchers have used is adoption studies. In theory, "adoption creates sets of genetically related individuals who do not share a common family environment because they were adopted apart".<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|page=80}} Adoption studies have broadly found that the IQs of adoptees are more similar to their biological parents than that of their adoptive parents,<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Turkheimer |first=Eric |date=November 1991 |title=Individual and group differences in adoption studies of IQ. |url=https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0033-2909.110.3.392 |journal=Psychological Bulletin |language=en |volume=110 |issue=3 |pages=392–405 |doi=10.1037/0033-2909.110.3.392 |issn=1939-1455 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250710083832/https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0033-2909.110.3.392 |archive-date=2025-07-10 |access-date=2025-10-14 |url-status=live }}</ref> in tandem with findings that adoption into better socioeconomic environments greatly increases IQ.<ref name=":38">{{Cite journal |last1=van IJzendoorn |first1=Marinus H. |last2=Juffer |first2=Femmie |last3=Poelhuis |first3=Caroline W. Klein |date=2005 |title=Adoption and Cognitive Development: A Meta-Analytic Comparison of Adopted and Nonadopted Children's IQ and School Performance. |url=https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0033-2909.131.2.301 |journal=Psychological Bulletin |language=en |volume=131 |issue=2 |pages=301–316 |doi=10.1037/0033-2909.131.2.301 |pmid=15740423 |issn=1939-1455 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250916131512/https://psycnet.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0033-2909.131.2.301 |archive-date=2025-09-16 |access-date=2025-10-14 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref name="ReferenceA">{{Cite journal |last1=Kendler |first1=Kenneth S. |last2=Turkheimer |first2=Eric |last3=Ohlsson |first3=Henrik |last4=Sundquist |first4=Jan |last5=Sundquist |first5=Kristina |date=2015-04-14 |title=Family environment and the malleability of cognitive ability: A Swedish national home-reared and adopted-away cosibling control study |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=112 |issue=15 |pages=4612–4617 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1417106112 |doi-access=free |pmc=4403216 |pmid=25831538 |bibcode=2015PNAS..112.4612K }}</ref> For example, one analysis of the Texas Adoption Project estimated heritability at 0.78.<ref name=":15">{{Cite book |last1=Loehlin |first1=John C. |author-link1=Thomas J. Bouchard Jr. |title=Intelligence, heredity, and environment |last2=Horn |first2=Joseph M. |last3=Willerman |first3=Lee |date=1999 |publisher=Cambridge Univ. Press |isbn=978-0-521-46904-3 |editor-last=Sternberg |editor-first=Robert J. |edition=Repr |location=Cambridge |pages=126–160 |chapter=Heredity, environment, and IQ in the Texas Adoption Project}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=123}} However, one recent adoption study estimate heritability for cognitive ability at 0.33.<ref>{{Cite report |title=Nature-Nurture Interplay: Evidence from Molecular Genetic and Pedigree Data in Korean American Adoptees |last1=Beauchamp |first1=Jonathan |last2=Schmitz |first2=Lauren |last3=McGue |first3=Matt |author-link3=Matt McGue |last4=Lee |first4=James |date=30 November 2023 |publisher=SSRN |doi=10.2139/ssrn.4491976 |ssrn=4491976 }}</ref> Some critics point to assortative mating, range restriction<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Stoolmiller |first=Mike |date=1998-11-01 |title=Correcting Estimates of Shared Environmental Variance for Range Restriction in Adoption Studies Using a Truncated Multivariate Normal Model |journal=Behavior Genetics |language=en |volume=28 |issue=6 |pages=429–441 |doi=10.1023/A:1021685211674 |issn=1573-3297 |pmid=9926612}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Stoolmiller |first=Mike |date=1999 |title=Implications of the restricted range of family environments for estimates of heritability and nonshared environment in behavior–genetic adoption studies. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0033-2909.125.4.392 |journal=Psychological Bulletin |language=en |volume=125 |issue=4 |pages=392–409 |doi=10.1037/0033-2909.125.4.392 |pmid=10414224 |issn=1939-1455|url-access=subscription }}</ref> and other complex family and social processes as providing issues in the interpretation of data from adoption studies.<ref name=":16" /><ref name=":37"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Burt |first1=S. ==== Other models ====
More broadly, researchers have analyzed the resemblance between various familial classes, such as parent-child correlations. In 1982, Bouchard and McGue reviewed such correlations reported in 111 original studies in the United States. The mean correlation of IQ scores between monozygotic twins was 0.86, between siblings 0.47, between half-siblings 0.31, and between cousins 0.15.<ref name="pmid7195071">{{cite journal |last1=Bouchard |first1=Thomas J. |last2=McGue |first2=Matthew |year=1981 |title=Familial Studies of Intelligence: A Review |journal=Science |volume=212 |issue=4498 |pages=1055–9 |bibcode=1981Sci...212.1055B |doi=10.1126/science.7195071 |pmid=7195071}}</ref> Some more basic model fitting studies are found in the behavioral genetics literature. Loehlin fit a model to the Bouchard and McGue data which estimated broad heritability at .58 from 'direct' methods and .47 from 'indirect' methods.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Loehlin |first=John C. |date=1989 |title=Partitioning environmental and genetic contributions to behavioral development. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0003-066X.44.10.1285 |journal=American Psychologist |language=en |volume=44 |issue=10 |pages=1285–1292 |doi=10.1037/0003-066X.44.10.1285 |pmid=2679255 |issn=1935-990X|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Plomin |first1=Robert |last2=Loehlin |first2=John C. |date=1989-05-01 |title=Direct and indirect IQ heritability estimates: A puzzle |journal=Behavior Genetics |language=en |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=331–342 |doi=10.1007/BF01066162 |pmid=2667514 |issn=1573-3297}}</ref> Chipuer et al. analyzed this data using a LISREL model and estimated broad sense heritability as .51.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chipuer |first1=Heather M. |last2=Rovine |first2=Michael J. |last3=Plomin |first3=Robert |date=1990-01-01 |title=LISREL modeling: Genetic and environmental influences on IQ revisited |journal=Intelligence |volume=14 |issue=1 |pages=11–29 |doi=10.1016/0160-2896(90)90011-H |issn=0160-2896}}</ref> Other models successively add more components. In 1997, Devlin et al. also used these correlations to fit and compare different models and estimated that heritability was less than 50% in their best fitting models, finding that [[maternal effect]]s were particularly important in their analysis.<ref name="devlin" /> Bouchard and McGue reviewed the literature in 2003, arguing that Devlin's conclusions about the magnitude of heritability is not substantially different from previous reports and that their conclusions regarding prenatal effects stands in contradiction to many previous reports.<ref name="pmid12486697">{{cite journal |last1=Bouchard |first1=Thomas J. |last2=McGue |first2=Matt |date=January 2003 |title=Genetic and environmental influences on human psychological differences |journal=Journal of Neurobiology |volume=54 |issue=1 |pages=4–45 |doi=10.1002/neu.10160 |pmid=12486697 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Genetics researchers observed that cultural heritability and genetic heritability can produce similar patterns of observations between relatives in the 1970s.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Shen |first1=Hao |last2=Feldman |first2=Marcus W. |date=2021-10-16 |title=Cultural versus biological inheritance: A retrospective view of Cavalli-Sforza and Feldman (1973) |url=https://www.pivotscipub.com/hpgg/1/1/0003/html |journal=Human Population Genetics and Genomics |language=en |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=1–18 |article-number=0003 |doi=10.47248/hpgg2101010003 |issn=2770-5005|doi-access=free }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Benning |first1=John W. |last2=Carlson |first2=Jedidiah |last3=Smith |first3=Olivia S. |last4=Shaw |first4=Ruth G. |last5=Harpak |first5=Arbel |date=2025-11-05 |title=Confounding fuels misinterpretation in human genetics |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society B: Biological Sciences |volume=292 |issue=2058 |article-number=20251615 |doi=10.1098/rspb.2025.1615 |pmc=12587318 |pmid=41190516}}</ref> As a result, in a series of papers using models based on path analysis, a group of researchers from the University of Hawaii analyzed data collected on American families and estimated genetic heritability ranging from 0.30 to 0.34.<ref name=":14" /><ref name=":30">{{Cite journal |last1=Rao |first1=D. === Molecular genetics ===
{{See also|Genome-wide association study|Polygenic score|Missing heritability problem}}

These findings are compatible with the view that a large number of genes, each with only a small effect, contribute to differences in intelligence.<ref name="Chabris">{{cite journal |last1=Chabris |first1=C. F. |last2=Hebert |first2=B. M. |last3=Benjamin |first3=D. J. |last4=Beauchamp |first4=J. |last5=Cesarini |first5=D. |last6=Van Der Loos |first6=M. |last7=Johannesson |first7=M. |last8=Magnusson |first8=P. K. Molecular genetic studies have been central to several major scientific advances relevant to heritability. The first is the advent of polygenic scores, which take the thousands of [[single-nucleotide polymorphism]]s (SNPs) that influence a given trait to form an estimated "genetic value" or "genetic propensity".<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rosenberg |first1=Noah A |last2=Edge |first2=Michael D |last3=Pritchard |first3=Jonathan K |last4=Feldman |first4=Marcus W |date=2018-12-27 |title=Interpreting polygenic scores, polygenic adaptation, and human phenotypic differences |url=https://academic.oup.com/emph/article/2019/1/26/5262222 |journal=Evolution, Medicine, and Public Health |language=en |volume=2019 |issue=1 |pages=26–34 |doi=10.1093/emph/eoy036 |pmid=30838127 |pmc=6393779 |issn=2050-6201 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250727113251/https://academic.oup.com/emph/article/2019/1/26/5262222 |archive-date=2025-07-27 |access-date=2025-10-14 |url-status=live }}</ref> Most genome-wide association studies (GWAS) estimate a polygenic score (PGS) and describe its overall statistical contribution to variance for the population in question, i.e. providing a R{{Sup|2}} ([[coefficient of determination]]) for the polygenic score.<ref name=":28">{{Cite book |last1=Mills |first1=Melinda |title=An introduction to statistical genetic data analysis |last2=Barban |first2=Nicola |last3=Tropf |first3=Felix C. |date=2020 |publisher=The MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-53838-1 |location=Cambridge, Massachusetts London, England}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=251}}<ref |language=en |volume=27 |issue=1 |pages=49–52 |doi=10.1038/s41380-021-01348-y |pmid=34686768 |pmc=8960389 |issn=1476-5578}}</ref> This measures only the predictive power of the genetic variants in the study in question, a future study with larger sample size or more genetic variants tagged may produce a larger amount.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Cesarini |first1=David |last2=Visscher |first2=Peter M. |date=2017-02-01 |title=Genetics and educational attainment |journal=npj Science of Learning |language=en |volume=2 |issue=1 |page=4 |doi=10.1038/s41539-017-0005-6  |doi-access=free|pmid=30631451 |pmc=6220209 |bibcode=2017npjSL...2....4C |issn=2056-7936}}</ref> Consequently, a given polygenic score only captures "a fraction of SNP-heritability".<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Pingault |first1=Jean-Baptiste |last2=Allegrini |first2=Andrea G. |last3=Odigie |first3=Tracy |last4=Frach |first4=Leonard |last5=Baldwin |first5=Jessie R. |last6=Rijsdijk |first6=Frühling |last7=Dudbridge Genomic studies have also estimated values of SNP heritability for IQ. Very early studies used a method called genome-wide complex trait analysis (GCTA) which calculates the overall genetic similarity (as indexed by the cumulative effects of all genotyped [[single nucleotide polymorphism]]s) between all pairs of individuals in a sample of unrelated individuals and then correlates this genetic similarity with phenotypic similarity across all the pairs.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Jian |last2=Lee |first2=S. == Environmental effects ==
=== Shared environment ===
{{See also|Causes of intelligence#Sociocultural}}
In biometrical studies that partition variance, "shared environment" refers to hypothetical factors that increase the similarity of relatives in a particular study design.<ref name=":36">{{Cite journal |last1=Daw |first1=Jonathan |last2=Guo |first2=Guang |last3=Harris |first3=Kathie Mullan |date=July 2015 |title=Nurture net of nature: Re-evaluating the role of shared environments in academic achievement and verbal intelligence |journal=Social Science Research |volume=52 |pages=422–439 |doi=10.1016/j.ssresearch.2015.02.011 |issn=1096-0317 |pmc=4888873 |pmid=26004471}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Harold |first=Goldsmith |title=Nature, Nurture, and Psychology |date=1993 |publisher=American Psychological Association |isbn=978-1-55798-202-5 |editor-last=Plomin |editor-first=Robert |editor-link=Robert Plomin |chapter=Nature–nurture issues in the behavioral genetics context: Overcoming barriers to communication. |editor-last2=McClearn |editor-first2=Gerald E. |editor-link2=Gerald E. McClearn |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/232479062}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=331-333}} Researchers draw a distinction between "objectively shared environments" (features of the environment that relatives such as siblings share) and the "shared environment" in behavioral genetics studies, which measures only the factors that increase homogeneity.<ref name=":36" /><ref>{{Citation |title=Shared and Nonshared Environment |date=2018 |encyclopedia=The SAGE Encyclopedia of Lifespan Human Development |url=https://sk.sagepub.com/reference/the-sage-encyclopedia-of-lifespan-human-development/i22712.xml |access-date=2025-10-28 |place=2455 Teller Road, Thousand Oaks, California 91320 |publisher=SAGE Publications, Inc. |doi=10.4135/9781506307633.n741 |isbn=978-1-5063-0765-7|url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref name=":41">{{Cite journal |last1=Turkheimer |first1=E. |last2=Waldron |first2=M. |date=January 2000 |title=Nonshared environment: a theoretical, methodological, and quantitative review |journal=Psychological Bulletin |volume=126 |issue=1 |pages=78–108 |doi=10.1037/0033-2909.126.1.78 |issn=0033-2909 |pmid=10668351}}</ref>

Researchers typically use the same designs to estimate shared environment effects as to estimate heritability: twin studies, adoption studies and family studies.<ref name=":37">{{Cite journal |last=Kaplan |first=Jack S. |date=2012 |title=The effects of shared environment on adult intelligence: A critical review of adoption, twin, and MZA studies. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/a0028133 |journal=Developmental Psychology |language=en |volume=48 |issue=5 |pages=1292–1298 |doi=10.1037/a0028133 |pmid=22746221 |issn=1939-0599|url-access=subscription }}</ref> These methods often come to disparate conclusions about the effects of shared environment.<ref name=":37" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Plomin |first1=R. |author-link1=Robert Plomin |last2=Loehlin |first2=J. C. |author-link2=John C. Loehlin |date=May 1985 |title=Direct and indirect IQ heritability estimates: a puzzle |journal=Behavior Genetics |volume=19 |issue=3 |pages=331–342 |doi=10.1007/BF01066162 |issn=0001-8244 |pmid=2667514}}</ref>

Some adoption studies show that by adulthood adoptive siblings aren't more similar in IQ than strangers,<ref name="PMIDCitationhas">{{cite journal |pmid=9549239 |year=1998 |last1=Bouchard Jr |first1=TJ |title=Genetic and environmental influences on adult intelligence and special mental abilities |volume=70 |issue=2 |pages=257–79 |journal=Human Biology}}</ref> while adult full siblings show an IQ correlation of 0.24. These findings have lead researchers such as Sandra Scarr and Robert Plomin to conclude that shared environment has minimal effect on intelligence in adulthood.<ref name=":37" />{{Reference page|page=1292|quote=The evidence most often cited in support of the claim that shared environment has little or no effect on adult intelligence comes from adoption studies}}<ref>{{Cite book |last=Scarr |first=Sandra |title=Intelligence, heredity, and environment |date=1999 |publisher=Cambridge Univ. Press |isbn=978-0-521-46904-3 |editor-last=Sternberg |editor-first=Robert J. |edition=Repr |location=Cambridge |chapter=Behavior-Genetic and Socialization theories of intelligence}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=27|quote=In contrast to the MZA studies, four studies of genetically unrelated
siblings adopted and reared from infancy to adulthood in the same homes
show sibling IQ correlations that range from .05 to -.03, with a median of
about 0.0. 
... 
Although estimates of shared nongenetic effects on individual differences in IQ from twin and adoption studies vary from 0 to 10%, one can say that they appear
to be rather small in adult populations in Western societies}} Psychologists [[Ken Richardson (psychologist)|Ken Richardson]] and Sarah Norgate question the assumptions of adoption studies for IQ, highlighting issues with assumptions of additivity and randomization.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Richardson |first1=Ken |last2=Norgate |first2=Sarah H. |date=2006 |title=A Critical Analysis of IQ Studies of Adopted Children |journal=Human Development |volume=49 |issue=6 |pages=319–335 |doi=10.1159/000096531 |jstor=26763905 |issn=0018-716X}}</ref> However, adoption studies have also shown that the process of adoption has a positive effect on IQ scores,<ref name=":38" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Duyme |first1=Michel |last2=Dumaret |first2=Annick-Camille |last3=Tomkiewicz |first3=Stanislaw |date=1999-07-20 |title=How can we boost IQs of "dull children"?: A late adoption study |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=96 |issue=15 |pages=8790–8794 |doi=10.1073/pnas.96.15.8790 |doi-access=free |pmc=17595 |pmid=10411954 |bibcode=1999PNAS...96.8790D }}</ref> and two studies have associated this with factors such as the level of parental education and [[socioeconomic status]] of adoptive parents.<ref name="ReferenceA"/><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Capron |first1=Christiane |last2=Duyme |first2=Michel |date=1996-05-01 |title=Effect of socioeconomic status of biological and adoptive parents on WISC-R subtest scores of their French adopted children |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0160289696900227 |journal=Intelligence |volume=22 |issue=3 |pages=259–275 |doi=10.1016/S0160-2896(96)90022-7 |issn=0160-2896|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In a 1991 paper, psychologist Eric Turkheimer tried to reconcile results from adoption studies that demonstrate large increases in IQ from adoption and those that show low correlations between non-biologically related relatives. He argued that early adoption studies first established that genetic effects influence behavioral phenotypes, while later studies from Schiff and colleagues demonstrate that environment has an influence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Turkheimer |first=Eric |date=November 1991 |title=Individual and group differences in adoption studies of IQ. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0033-2909.110.3.392 |journal=Psychological Bulletin |language=en |volume=110 |issue=3 |pages=392–405 |doi=10.1037/0033-2909.110.3.392 |issn=1939-1455|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Researchers Alexandra Burt and Wendy Johnson argue that the joint study of means and variance is necessary to understand the impact of environment.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Burt |first1=S. Alexandra |last2=Johnson |first2=Wendy |date=2023-03-01 |title=Joint Consideration of Means and Variances Might Change the Understanding of Etiology |journal=Perspectives on Psychological Science |language=EN |volume=18 |issue=2 |pages=416–427 |doi=10.1177/17456916221096122 |pmid=36027892 |issn=1745-6916 |url=https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/7a7640e3-3b29-446f-86df-bae2be55729e |hdl=20.500.11820/7a7640e3-3b29-446f-86df-bae2be55729e |hdl-access=free }}</ref> In a 2024 study, Burt et al. propose that measurement error or noise might inhibit the identification of specific environmental factors that influence academic achievement.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Burt |first1=S. Alexandra |last2=O'Keefe |first2=Patrick |last3=Johnson |first3=Wendy |last4=Thaler |first4=Daniel |last5=Leve |first5=Leslie D. |last6=Natsuaki |first6=Misaki N. |last7=Reiss |first7=David |last8=Shaw |first8=Daniel S. |last9=Ganiban |first9=Jody M. |last10=Neiderhiser |first10=Jenae M. |date=2024-05-01 |title=The Detection of Environmental Influences on Academic Achievement Appears to Depend on the Analytic Approach |journal=Behavior Genetics |language=en |volume=54 |issue=3 |pages=252–267 |doi=10.1007/s10519-024-10179-w |pmid=38587720 |issn=1573-3297 |url=https://www.research.ed.ac.uk/en/publications/f0fcb32e-710e-4ab4-b4a9-c84b4ea046e9 }}</ref>
[[File:Sundet et al data.png|thumb|Relationship between correlation between brothers' IQ scores and age differences in Sundet et al. 2008<ref name=":42" />]]
Some studies of twins reared apart (e.g. Bouchard, 1990) find a significant shared environmental influence, of at least 10% going into late adulthood.<ref name="BibcodeSciBCitationhas">{{cite journal |last1=Bouchard |first1=Thomas J. |last2=Lykken |first2=David T. |last3=McGue |first3=Matthew |last4=Segal |first4=Nancy L. |last5=Tellegen |first5=Auke |year=1990 |title=Sources of Human Psychological Differences: The Minnesota Study of Twins Reared Apart |journal=Science |volume=250 |issue=4978 |pages=223–8 |bibcode=1990Sci...250..223B |doi=10.1126/science.2218526 |pmid=2218526}}</ref> Jack Kaplan suggests that the evidence from twin studies and adoption studies are inconsistent, and that twin studies suggest a role for the effect of shared environment on intelligence in adulthood.<ref name=":37" /> Researchers such as Briley and Tucker-Drob have suggested that low shared environmental estimates in adulthood may arise because individuals differentially respond to objectively shared environments over time, as a result of unmodelled interactions with either genetic or objectively nonshared environmental factors.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Briley |first1=Daniel A. |last2=Tucker-Drob |first2=Elliot M. |date=February 2017 |title=Comparing the Developmental Genetics of Cognition and Personality over the Life Span |journal=Journal of Personality |volume=85 |issue=1 |pages=51–64 |doi=10.1111/jopy.12186 |issn=1467-6494 |pmc=4670606 |pmid=26045299}}</ref> One unpublished [[meta-analysis]] of twin studies finds estimates of shared environment around 20% for 15-20 year olds, but results for adults no greater than 15%.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Dickens |first1=William T. |title=The Heritability of Cognitive Ability Across the Lifespan: A Meta-Analysis of Twins Studies |date=2015-10-23 |type=SSRN Scholarly Paper |place=Rochester, NY |language=en |id=2679002 |last2=Protzko |first2=John |ssrn=2679002 }}</ref>{{Better source needed|reason=The current source is insufficiently reliable ([[WP:NOTRS]]).|date=October 2025}} Researchers have proposed many different factors that could influence intelligence through the shared environment component. One 2018 paper by Laura Engelhardt and colleagues found that measures of socioeconomic status, school demographics and neighborhood socioeconomic status statistically account for most of shared environmental influences on several metrics of intelligence.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Engelhardt |first1=Laura E. |last2=Church |first2=Jessica A. |last3=Paige Harden |first3=K. |last4=Tucker-Drob |first4=Elliot M. |date=Aug 2018 |title=Accounting for the shared environment in cognitive abilities and academic achievement with measured socioecological contexts |journal=Developmental Science |volume=22 |issue=1 |article-number=e12699 |doi=10.1111/desc.12699 |issn=1467-7687 |pmc=6294670 |pmid=30113118}}</ref>

Another method researchers have used to estimate the shared environmental component for intelligence is studies of siblings. In a large study, Kendler and colleagues used twins, step-siblings, and half-siblings to estimate the shared environment component of many behavioral phenotypes. They found shared environment components for IQ ranging from about 10% to 20%, depending on the relationship class.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kendler |first1=Kenneth S. |last2=Ohlsson |first2=Henrik |last3=Lichtenstein |first3=Paul |last4=Sundquist |first4=Jan |last5=Sundquist |first5=Kristina |date=2019-01-01 |title=The Nature of the Shared Environment |journal=Behavior Genetics |language=en |volume=49 |issue=1 |pages=1–10 |doi=10.1007/s10519-018-9940-0 |pmid=30536082 |issn=1573-3297}}</ref>{{Reference page|location=Fig 1.}} Another study found an association between similarity in age between siblings and similarity in IQ scores, suggesting familial environment influences on intelligence scores.<ref name=":42">{{Cite journal |last1=Sundet |first1=Jon Martin |last2=Eriksen |first2=Willy |last3=Tambs |first3=Kristian |date=September 2008 |title=Intelligence correlations between brothers decrease with increasing age difference: evidence for shared environmental effects in young adults |journal=Psychological Science |volume=19 |issue=9 |pages=843–847 |doi=10.1111/j.1467-9280.2008.02166.x |issn=1467-9280 |pmid=18947347}}</ref>

A 2015 study by Johnathan Daw and colleagues argues that the additivity assumption of typical family studies is not correct and that measures of objectively measured shared environment could moderate the estimated nonshared environment component. They found that shared environments such as [[birth order]], household size, sibling age dispersion, and school quality exhibit "large moderating effects on both verbal intelligence and academic achievement". They suggested that these results show how objectively shared environments can influence intelligence in contrast to a common belief that objectively shared environments do not influence children's lives.<ref name=":36" />

=== Non-shared environment ===
As nonshared environmental variance is simply the leftover variance not accounted for by genetic variance and shared environmental variance, it encompasses any factors that cause differences between siblings and estimates vary based on the estimates of heritability and shared environment.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Plomin |first1=Robert |author-link1=Robert Plomin |title=Separate Social Worlds of Siblings |last2=Chipuer |first2=Heather |last3=Neiderhiser |first3=Jenae M. |date=1994 |publisher=Routledge |isbn=978-1-138-98166-9 |editor-last=Hetherington |editor-first=E. Mavis |edition=1st |chapter=Behavioral genetic evidence for the importance of nonshared environment |editor-last2=Reiss |editor-first2=David |editor-last3=Plomin |editor-first3=Robert |editor-link3=Robert Plomin |chapter-url=https://d1wqtxts1xzle7.cloudfront.net/112662728/1994-hetherington-separatesocialworldsofsiblings-libre.pdf?1711580030=&response-content-disposition=inline%3B+filename%3DSeparate_Social_Worlds_of_Siblings.pdf&Expires=1761810205&Signature=U70p9rrCHgEh9BL9oD0gP1A57wLXJO9vf3QW2oAoHC6S9QmK4Z6546K5xT0dGXxVeVgCIBaxU98USSwL~FQjz0FfgvnJBnuB4hu2AgzvzMTqf2tUdQmp5HeM1TchmRMO4cS37WCi3ukmGL5RPg1n9kiwDanh8Nhu370s2Y-Xm7LyhUvsa5cd-a1U~kOxhxneT1j5j-s55UoCtnj2oy6G9X6iBZ8AqBlL8DJokZujDXvndMSdf7UkDVyJ4Tv3u2hMEmMkCHs2Ww4oNnDXe-WEJL5TwJYFZRgDaGbP8DYzrftLq11ALaRpjABjlhVdJ9EIbHjDmbScEB~x1BWj7i1eDA__&Key-Pair-Id=APKAJLOHF5GGSLRBV4ZA#page=9}}</ref>{{Reference page|page=22}} Robert McCall argues nonshared environment contributes 15-25% of the variance of IQ scores.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=McCall |first=Robert B. |date=1983 |title=Environmental Effects on Intelligence: The Forgotten Realm of Discontinuous Nonshared Within-Family Factors |journal=Child Development |volume=54 |issue=2 |pages=408–415 |doi=10.2307/1129701 |jstor=1129701 |pmid=6872632 |issn=0009-3920}}</ref> Although parents treat their children differently, known measures of differential treatment explains only a small amount of non-shared environmental influence.<ref name=":41" /><ref name="Plomin0103">{{cite journal |last1=Plomin |first1=R |last2=Asbury |first2=K |last3=Dunn |first3=J |year=2001 |title=Why are children in the same family so different? Nonshared environment a decade later |journal=Canadian Journal of Psychiatry |volume=46 |issue=3 |pages=225–33 |doi=10.1177/070674370104600302 |pmid=11320676 |doi-access=free}}</ref> One suggestion is that children react differently to the same environmental factors: that objectively shared measures of the environment can have different effects on siblings.<ref name=":41" />{{Reference page|page=79|quote=Thus, if an objectively shared environmental variable results in nonshared effects, the effective contribution of the objectively shared event is included with the nonshared rather then the shared component of variance. Consider, for example, parental divorce. Like most other traditional between-family environmental variables, parental divorce is usually an objectively shared event. It is possible, however, that objectively shared events may have different effects on siblings.}} One 1994 study of the National Longitudinal Survey of Youth found that a measure of the home environment accounted for nonshared environmental variance for several measures of intelligence,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rodgers |first1=Joseph Lee |last2=Rowe |first2=David C. |last3=May |first3=Kim |date=1994-09-01 |title=DF analysis of NLSY IQ/achievement data: Nonshared environmental influences |journal=Intelligence |volume=19 |issue=2 |pages=157–177 |doi=10.1016/0160-2896(94)90011-6 |issn=0160-2896}}</ref> while Daw et al. suggest that nonshared environment is moderated by objectively shared environment.<ref name=":36" /> More likely influences may be the impact of peers and other experiences outside the family.<ref name="unknown" /> For example, siblings grown up in the same household may have different friends and teachers and even contract different illnesses. This factor may be one of the reasons why IQ score correlations between siblings decreases as they get older.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Schacter |first1=Daniel |first2=Daniel |last2=Gilbert |first3=Daniel |last3=Wegner |title=Psychology |url=https://archive.org/details/psychology0000scha |url-access=registration |edition=2nd |location=New York |publisher=Worth Publishers |year=2010 |page=[https://archive.org/details/psychology0000scha/page/408 408] |isbn=978-1-4292-3719-2}}</ref>

Some authors highlight measurement error as one source of variance attributed to the nonshared environment, as measurement error is captured in the nonshared environment term.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Plomin |first=Robert |date=September 2024 |title=Nonshared environment: Real but random |journal=JCPP Advances |volume=4 |issue=3 |article-number=e12229 |doi=10.1002/jcv2.12229 |doi-access=free |issn=2692-9384 |pmc=11472802 |pmid=39411468}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Gang |last2=Moraczewski |first2=Dustin |last3=Taylor |first3=Paul A. |date=2025-04-02 |title=Improving accuracy and precision of heritability estimation in twin studies through hierarchical modeling: reassessing the measurement error assumption |journal=Frontiers in Genetics |language=English |volume=16 |article-number=1522729 |doi=10.3389/fgene.2025.1522729 |pmid=40242473 |pmc=11999965 |doi-access=free |issn=1664-8021}}</ref> Another factor that produces differences between individuals is stochastic variation, often attributed to nonlinear epigenetic processes.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Molenaar |first1=Peter C. M. |last2=Boomsma |first2=Dorret I. |last3=Dolan |first3=Conor V. |date=1993-11-01 |title=A third source of developmental differences |journal=Behavior Genetics |language=en |volume=23 |issue=6 |pages=519–524 |doi=10.1007/BF01068142 |pmid=8129693 |issn=1573-3297 |url=https://research.vu.nl/en/publications/292d0376-7da1-4ac7-8d8c-0ae19f195465 }}</ref><ref>{{Citation |last=Vogt |first=Günter |chapter=9 - Disentangling the environmentally induced and stochastic developmental components of phenotypic variation |date=2020-01-01 |title=Phenotypic Switching |pages=207–251 |editor-last=Levine |editor-first=Herbert |chapter-url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/B9780128179963000104 |access-date=2025-10-30 |publisher=Academic Press |isbn=978-0-12-817996-3 |editor2-last=Jolly |editor2-first=Mohit Kumar |editor3-last=Kulkarni |editor3-first=Prakash |editor4-last=Nanjundiah |editor4-first=Vidyanand}}</ref>

=== Dickens and Flynn model ===

Dickens and Flynn (2001) argued that the "heritability" figure includes both a direct effect of the [[genotype]] on IQ and also indirect effects where the genotype changes the environment, in turn affecting IQ. That is, those with a higher IQ tend to seek out stimulating environments that further increase IQ. The direct effect can initially have been very small but [[feedback]] loops can create large differences in IQ. In their model an environmental stimulus can have a very large effect on IQ, even in adults, but this effect also decays over time unless the stimulus continues.<ref name="DickensFlynn2001">{{cite journal |last1=Dickens |first1=William T. |last2=Flynn |first2=James R. |year=2001 |title=Heritability estimates versus large environmental effects: The IQ paradox resolved |journal=Psychological Review |volume=108 |issue=2 |pages=346–69 |doi=10.1037/0033-295X.108.2.346 |pmid=11381833}}</ref> This model could be adapted to include possible factors, like nutrition in early childhood, that may cause permanent effects.{{citation needed|date=December 2025}}

The [[Flynn effect]] is the increase in average intelligence test scores by about 0.3% annually, resulting in the average person today scoring 15 points higher in IQ compared to the generation 50 years ago.<ref name="Schacter409">{{cite book |last1=Schacter |first1=Daniel |url=https://archive.org/details/psychology0000scha |title=Psychology |last2=Gilbert |first2=Daniel |last3=Wegner |first3=Daniel |publisher=Worth Publishers |year=2010 |isbn=978-1-4292-3719-2 |edition=2nd |location=New York |pages=[https://archive.org/details/psychology0000scha/page/409 409–10] |url-access=registration}}</ref> This effect can be explained by a generally more stimulating environment for all people.
Some scientists have suggested that such enhancements are due to better nutrition, better parenting and schooling, as well as exclusion of the least intelligent people from reproduction. However, Flynn and a group of other scientists share the viewpoint that modern life implies solving many abstract problems which leads to a rise in their IQ scores.<ref name="Schacter409" />

=== Indirect genetic effects ===

Various molecular genetic studies have identified an effect of alleles not carried by an individual, but some relative, on their phenotype.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bijma |first=P. |date=January 2014 |title=The quantitative genetics of indirect genetic effects: a selective review of modelling issues |journal=Heredity |language=en |volume=112 |issue=1 |pages=61–69 |doi=10.1038/hdy.2013.15 |pmid=23512010 |pmc=3860160 |bibcode=2014Hered.112...61B |issn=1365-2540}}</ref> These have been varyingly referred to as "dynastic effects",<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Brumpton |first1=Ben
