Kong<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kong |first1=Augustine |last2=Thorleifsson |first2=Gudmar |last3=Frigge |first3=Michael L. |last4=Vilhjalmsson |first4=Bjarni J. |last5=Young |first5=Alexander I. |last6=Thorgeirsson |first6=Thorgeir E. |last7=Benonisdottir |first7=Stefania |last8=Oddsson |first8=Asmundur |last9=Halldorsson |first9=Bjarni V. |last10=Masson |first10=Gisli |last11=Gudbjartsson |first11=Daniel F. |last12=Helgason |first12=Agnar |last13=Bjornsdottir |first13=Gyda |last14=Thorsteinsdottir |first14=Unnur |last15=Stefansson |first15=Kari |date=25 January 2018 |title=The nature of nurture: Effects of parental genotypes |journal=Science |volume=359 |issue=6374 |pages=424–428 |bibcode=2018Sci...359..424K |doi=10.1126/science.aan6877 |pmid=29371463 |doi-access=free}}</ref> reports that, "Nurture has a genetic component, i.e. alleles in the parents affect the parents' phenotypes and through that influence the outcomes of the child." These results were obtained through a meta-analysis of [[educational attainment]] and [[Polygene|polygenic]] scores of non-transmitted alleles. Although the study deals with educational attainment and not IQ, these two are strongly linked.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Deary |first1=Ian J. |last2=Strand |first2=Steve |last3=Smith |first3=Pauline |last4=Fernandes |first4=Cres |date=January 2007 |title=Intelligence and educational achievement |journal=Intelligence |volume=35 |issue=1 |pages=13–21 |doi=10.1016/j.intell.2006.02.001}}</ref>

== Influences ==

=== Heritability and socioeconomic status ===
{{See also|Scarr–Rowe effect|Causes of intelligence#Family}}
Hypotheses about the relationship between the value of heritability and socioeconomic status originated with [[Sandra Scarr]]'s 1971 article Race, Social Class, and IQ.<ref name=":35">{{Cite journal |last=Scarr-Salapatek |first=Sandra |date=1971-12-24 |title=Race, Social Class, and IQ |url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.174.4016.1285 |journal=Science |volume=174 |issue=4016 |pages=1285–1295 |doi=10.1126/science.174.4016.1285 |pmid=5167501 |bibcode=1971Sci...174.1285S |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Scarr notes that existing theories of environmental disadvantage explaining the relationship between social class and IQ predict that more advantaged groups will show greater genetic variance as the advantaged groups don't experience as many detrimental environmental effects. In her study, she identified statistical interactions between socioeconomic environment and genetic variance, finding that genetic influences on IQ were stronger in higher socioeconomic groups where environmental conditions allowed genetic potential to be more fully expressed, whereas in lower socioeconomic groups, adverse environments constrained this expression and reduced the impact of genetic differences.<ref name=":1" /><ref name=":35" /> Other than some minor criticisms and a partial replication, the topic was not broached again until the 1996 APA report "[[Intelligence: Knowns and Unknowns]]",<ref name=":1" /> which stated that: <blockquote>
"We should note, however, that [[Poverty|low-income]] and non-white families are poorly represented in existing adoption studies as well as in most twin samples. Thus it is not yet clear whether these studies apply to the population as a whole. It remains possible that, across the full range of income and ethnicity, between-family differences have more lasting consequences for psychometric intelligence."<ref name="unknown"/>
</blockquote>
[[File:Relationship between SES and heritability of IQ.png|thumb|Relationship between the genetic variance component and socioeconomic status in Turkheimer et al. 2003<ref name="Turkheimer2003" />]]
A 1999 study by [[David C. Rowe|David Rowe]] and colleagues replicated the effect in the [[National Longitudinal Study of Adolescent Health]], finding that among children from poorly-educated parents 'shared environment' was associated with most of the variance, while among children from well-educated parents, genes were associated with most of the variance.<ref name=":1" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rowe |first1=D. C. |last2=Jacobson |first2=K. C. |last3=Van den Oord |first3=E. J. |date=1999 |title=Genetic and environmental influences on vocabulary IQ: parental education level as moderator |journal=Child Development |volume=70 |issue=5 |pages=1151–1162 |doi=10.1111/1467-8624.00084 |issn=0009-3920 |pmid=10546338}}</ref> Turkheimer and colleagues (2003) argued that the proportions of IQ variance attributable to genes and environment vary with socioeconomic status. They found that in a study on seven-year-old twins, in impoverished families, 60% of the variance in early childhood IQ was accounted for by the shared family environment, and the contribution of genes is close to zero; in affluent families, the result is almost exactly the reverse.<ref name="Turkheimer2003">{{cite journal |last1=Turkheimer |first1=Eric |author-link=Eric Turkheimer |last2=Haley |first2=Andreana |last3=Waldron |first3=Mary |last4=d'Onofrio |first4=Brian |last5=Gottesman |first5=Irving I. |year=2003 |title=Socioeconomic status modifies heritability of iq in young children |journal=Psychological Science |volume=14 |issue=6 |pages=623–8 |doi=10.1046/j.0956-7976.2003.psci_1475.x |pmid=14629696 |s2cid=11265284}}</ref> The name "Scarr-Rowe effect" was proposed for this proposed interaction between heritability and socioeconomic status by [[Eric Turkheimer]] in 2009 paper presentation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Giangrande |first1=Evan J. |last2=Turkheimer |first2=Eric |date=May 2022 |title=Race, Ethnicity, and the Scarr-Rowe Hypothesis: A Cautionary Example of Fringe Science Entering the Mainstream |url=https://osf.io/preprints/psyarxiv/md3qw_v1 |journal=Perspectives on Psychological Science: A Journal of the Association for Psychological Science |volume=17 |issue=3 |pages=696–710 |doi=10.1177/17456916211017498 |issn=1745-6924 |pmid=34793248}}</ref> Later studies found more equivocal results, some failing to replicate the finding in different locations. A 2016 meta-analysis found that the effects varied by country, with moderate interactions in studies from the United States, while the effects were zero or reversed in studies from Australia and Western Europe.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Tucker-Drob |first1=Elliot M. |last2=Bates |first2=Timothy C. |date=Feb 2016 |title=Large Cross-National Differences in Gene × Socioeconomic Status Interaction on Intelligence |journal=Psychological Science |volume=27 |issue=2 |pages=138–149 |doi=10.1177/0956797615612727 |issn=1467-9280 |pmc=4749462 |pmid=26671911}}</ref> A large study published the following year, however, found negligible impacts using data from twins in Florida.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Figlio |first1=David N. |last2=Freese |first2=Jeremy |last3=Karbownik |first3=Krzysztof |last4=Roth |first4=Jeffrey |date=2017-12-19 |title=Socioeconomic status and genetic influences on cognitive development |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=114 |issue=51 |pages=13441–13446 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1708491114 |doi-access=free |pmc=5754768 |pmid=29133413 |bibcode=2017PNAS..11413441F }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mills |first1=Melinda C. |last2=Tropf |first2=Felix C. |date=2020-07-30 |title=Sociology, Genetics, and the Coming of Age of Sociogenomics |url=https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev-soc-121919-054756 |journal=Annual Review of Sociology |language=en |volume=46 |issue=46 |pages=553–581 |doi=10.1146/annurev-soc-121919-054756 |issn=0360-0572|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

Recent research has focused on the relationship between socioeconomic status and heritability using genomic data. One 2020 study on educational attainment, a closely related but not identical [[phenotype]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Krapohl |first1=Eva |last2=Rimfeld |first2=Kaili |last3=Shakeshaft |first3=Nicholas G. |last4=Trzaskowski |first4=Maciej |last5=McMillan |first5=Andrew |last6=Pingault |first6=Jean-Baptiste |last7=Asbury |first7=Kathryn |last8=Harlaar |first8=Nicole |last9=Kovas |first9=Yulia |last10=Dale |first10=Philip S. |last11=Plomin |first11=Robert |date=2014-10-21 |title=The high heritability of educational achievement reflects many genetically influenced traits, not just intelligence |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=111 |issue=42 |pages=15273–15278 |doi=10.1073/pnas.1408777111 |doi-access=free |pmc=4210287 |pmid=25288728 |bibcode=2014PNAS..11115273K }}</ref> found that polygenic scores had greater predictive value in lower socioeconomic status quartiles.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Mostafavi |first1=Hakhamanesh |last2=Harpak |first2=Arbel |last3=Agarwal |first3=Ipsita |last4=Conley |first4=Dalton |last5=Pritchard |first5=Jonathan K |last6=Przeworski |first6=Molly |date=2020-01-30 |title=Variable prediction accuracy of polygenic scores within an ancestry group |journal=eLife |language=en |volume=9 |article-number=e48376 |doi=10.7554/eLife.48376 |pmid=31999256 |pmc=7067566 |doi-access=free |issn=2050-084X}}</ref> A 2021 study similarly found an increase in SNP heritability with increasing socioeconomic deprivation; lower socioeconomic status was associated with higher heritability.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Rask-Andersen |first1=Mathias |last2=Karlsson |first2=Torgny |last3=Ek |first3=Weronica E. |last4=Johansson |first4=Åsa |date=July 2021 |title=Modification of Heritability for Educational Attainment and Fluid Intelligence by Socioeconomic Deprivation in the UK Biobank |url=https://psychiatryonline.org/doi/10.1176/appi.ajp.2020.20040462 |journal=American Journal of Psychiatry |volume=178 |issue=7 |pages=625–634 |doi=10.1176/appi.ajp.2020.20040462 |pmid=33900812 |issn=0002-953X|url-access=subscription }}</ref> One 2024 study used polygenic indices and found that the Scarr-Rowe hypothesis "lacks empirical support" and suggested an alternative theory, the compensatory advantage hypothesis, that heritability was ''lower'' among populations with higher heritability.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Ghirardi |first1=Gaia |last2=Gil-Hernández |first2=Carlos J. |last3=Bernardi |first3=Fabrizio |last4=van Bergen |first4=Elsje |last5=Demange |first5=Perline |date=2024-08-01 |title=Interaction of family SES with children's genetic propensity for cognitive and noncognitive skills: No evidence of the Scarr-Rowe hypothesis for educational outcomes |journal=Research in Social Stratification and Mobility |volume=92 |article-number=100960 |doi=10.1016/j.rssm.2024.100960 |pmid=39220821 |pmc=11364161 |issn=0276-5624}}</ref>

=== Heritability and age ===
[[File:Twin correlations over development.png|thumb|Twin correlations over development (data from Wilson 1983<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wilson |first=Ronald S. |date=1983 |title=The Louisville Twin Study: Developmental Synchronies in Behavior |journal=Child Development |volume=54 |issue=2 |pages=298–316 |doi=10.2307/1129693 |jstor=1129693 |pmid=6683617 |issn=0009-3920}}</ref>)]]
The interaction between heritability and age over the course of development has been the interest of scientists for many years. Perhaps first described by Ronald Wilson,<ref name=":29">{{Cite journal |last=Bouchard |first=Thomas J. |date=October 2013 |title=The Wilson Effect: the increase in heritability of IQ with age |journal=Twin Research and Human Genetics|volume=16 |issue=5 |pages=923–930 |doi=10.1017/thg.2013.54 |issn=1832-4274 |pmid=23919982}}</ref> researchers have noted changes in kinship correlations over the life course. Particularly in the case of twins, the correlation between monozygotic twins remains relatively constant, while the correlation between dizygotic twins decreases.<ref name=":29" />{{Reference page|pages=923}} Some early attempts at modeling this change have equivocal results, with Rao et al. finding that heritability increased in adulthood in one model, but not in another,<ref name=":30" /> while a later study by Devlin et al. did not find support for age moderation of heritability.<ref name="devlin" /> Most researchers in behavioral genetics now believe that estimates of heritability from classical family studies (adoption, twin studies) increase as individuals age,<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|pages=179-183}}.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Haworth |first1=C. M. A. |last2=Wright |first2=M. J. |last3=Luciano |first3=M. |last4=Martin |first4=N. G. |last5=de Geus |first5=E. J. C. |last6=van Beijsterveldt |first6=C. E. M. |last7=Bartels |first7=M. |last8=Posthuma |first8=D. |last9=Boomsma |first9=D. I. |last10=Davis |first10=O. S. P. |last11=Kovas |first11=Y. |last12=Corley |first12=R. P. |last13=Defries |first13=J. C. |last14=Hewitt |first14=J. K. |last15=Olson |first15=R. K. |date=2 June 2009 |title=The heritability of general cognitive ability increases linearly from childhood to young adulthood |journal=Molecular Psychiatry |volume=15 |issue=11 |pages=1112–1120 |doi=10.1038/mp.2009.55 |issn=1476-5578 |pmc=2889158 |pmid=19488046}}</ref>{{Clarify|reason="Most researchers believe" isn't supported by the text, need to reword|date=November 2025}} One review described a "linearly increasing heritability of intelligence from infancy (20%) through adulthood (60%)".<ref name=":31">{{Cite journal |last1=Plomin |first1=Robert |last2=DeFries |first2=John C. |last3=Knopik |first3=Valerie S. |last4=Neiderhiser |first4=Jenae M. |date=2016-01-01 |title=Top 10 Replicated Findings From Behavioral Genetics |journal=Perspectives on Psychological Science |language=EN |volume=11 |issue=1 |pages=3–23 |doi=10.1177/1745691615617439 |issn=1745-6916 |pmc=4739500 |pmid=26817721}}</ref><ref name=":39">{{Cite journal |last1=Reis |first1=André |last2=Spinath |first2=Frank M. |date=2025-01-24 |title=The Genetics of Intelligence |journal=Deutsches Arzteblatt International |volume=122 |issue=2 |pages=38–42 |doi=10.3238/arztebl.m2024.0236 |issn=1866-0452 |pmc=12416016 |pmid=39635948}}</ref> This increase in heritability with age is known as the "Wilson Effect".<ref name=":29" /> There are two possible explanations for why measured heritability might increase over the course of the lifespan: that new genetic factors are activated (genetic innovation) or that previous genetic factors explain more variance (genetic amplification).<ref name=":31" /><ref name=":32" /> Behavioral genetics researchers believe that genetic amplification is most supported by the evidence,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Plomin |first1=R. |last2=Deary |first2=I. J. |date=February 2015 |title=Genetics and intelligence differences: five special findings |journal=Molecular Psychiatry |language=en |volume=20 |issue=1 |pages=98–108 |doi=10.1038/mp.2014.105 |pmid=25224258 |pmc=4270739 |issn=1476-5578}}</ref> where the same genetic factors that influence IQ at one age are involved later, but produce larger and larger phenotypic effects over time.<ref name=":4" />{{Reference page|page=182}}<ref name=":32">{{Cite journal |last1=Briley |first1=Daniel A. |last2=Tucker-Drob |first2=Elliot M. |date=1 July 2013 |title=Explaining the increasing heritability of cognitive ability across development: a meta-analysis of longitudinal twin and adoption studies |journal=Psychological Science |volume=24 |issue=9 |pages=1704–1713 |doi=10.1177/0956797613478618 |issn=1467-9280 |pmc=3954471 |pmid=23818655}}</ref> One theory proposed to explain the apparent increase in heritability values is a reciprocal effects model, where environments and genes become correlated over the course of development.<ref name="DickensFlynn2001" /><ref name=":39" /><ref>{{Cite book |title=The dynamic genome and mental health: The role of genes and environments in youth development |publisher=Oxford University Press |year=2011 |isbn=978-0-19-973796-3 |editor-last=Kendler |editor-first=Kenneth S. |location=USA |pages=103–127 |language=en-US |chapter=The Social Dynamics of the Expression of Genes for Cognitive Ability |editor-last2=Jaffree |editor-first2=Sara |editor-last3=Romer |editor-first3=Daniel |chapter-url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/292759039}}</ref> These models incorporate phenotype to environment associations that violate the independence assumption in traditional behavioral genetic models that may overestimate heritability.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Beam |first1=Christopher R. |last2=Pezzoli |first2=Patrizia |last3=Mendle |first3=Jane |last4=Burt |first4=S. Alexandra |last5=Neale |first5=Michael C. |last6=Boker |first6=Steven M. |last7=Keel |first7=Pamela K. |last8=Klump |first8=Kelly L. |date=Feb 2022 |title=How nonshared environmental factors come to correlate with heredity |journal=Development and Psychopathology |volume=34 |issue=1 |pages=321–333 |doi=10.1017/S0954579420001017 |issn=1469-2198 |pmc=8081739 |pmid=33118912}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Beam |first1=Christopher R. |last2=Turkheimer |first2=Eric |date=Feb 2013 |title=Phenotype-environment correlations in longitudinal twin models |journal=Development and Psychopathology |volume=25 |issue=1 |pages=7–16 |doi=10.1017/S0954579412000867 |issn=1469-2198 |pmc=5746192 |pmid=23398749}}</ref> Another proposed explanation for why measured heritability can increase over the course of development is gene-environment interactions.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Fischbein |first=Siv |date=1978-12-01 |title=Heredity-Environment Interaction in the Development of Twins |journal=International Journal of Behavioral Development |language=EN |volume=1 |issue=4 |pages=313–322 |doi=10.1177/016502547800100402 |issn=0165-0254}}</ref>

Recent molecular genetics research has also investigated the interaction between genetics or heritability and age over the course of development. One 2018 genome-wide association study found "comparable heritability across age".<ref name=":33" /> Another study found that the within-family estimate heritability was 0.12 in childhood, 0.13 in adolescence and 0.15 in adulthood.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Lin |first1=Yujing |last2=Procopio |first2=Francesca |last3=Keser |first3=Engin |last4=Kawakami |first4=Kaito |last5=Rimfeld |first5=Kaili |last6=Malanchini |first6=Margherita |last7=Plomin |first7=Robert |date=2025-06-23 |title=Polygenic Score Prediction Within and Between Sibling Pairs for Intelligence, Cognitive Abilities, and Educational Traits From Childhood to Early Adulthood |url=https://icajournal.scholasticahq.com/article/140654-polygenic-score-prediction-within-and-between-sibling-pairs-for-intelligence-cognitive-abilities-and-educational-traits-from-childhood-to-early-adul |journal=Intelligence & Cognitive Abilities |language=en |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=5–19 |doi=10.65550/001c.140654 }}</ref>

== Implications ==

=== Development ===
Some researchers, especially those that work in fields like [[developmental systems theory]], have criticized the concept of heritability as misleading or meaningless. [[Douglas Wahlsten]] and [[Gilbert Gottlieb]] argue that the prevailing models of behavioral genetics are too simplistic by not accounting for gene-environment interactions.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Wahlsten |first1=Douglas |title=Intelligence, heredity, and environment |last2=Gottlieb |first2=Gilbert |date=1999 |publisher=Cambridge Univ. Press |isbn=978-0-521-46904-3 |editor-last=Sternberg |editor-first=Robert J. |edition=Repr |location=Cambridge |chapter=The invalid separation of effects of nature and nurture: Lessons from animal experimentation}}</ref> Stephen Ceci also highlights the issues with this assumption, noting that they were first raised by Jane Loevinger in 1943.<ref name=":19" />{{Reference page|pages=139-141}}<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Loevinger |first=J. |date=December 1943 |title=On the proportional contributions of differences in nature and in nurture to differences in intelligence. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/h0053767 |journal=Psychological Bulletin |language=en |volume=40 |issue=10 |pages=725–756 |doi=10.1037/h0053767 |issn=1939-1455|url-access=subscription }}</ref> They assert that the idea of partitioning variance makes no sense when environments and genes interact and argue that such interaction is ubiquitous in human development.<ref name=":18">{{Cite journal |last1=Moore |first1=David S. |last2=Shenk |first2=David |date=January 2017 |title=The heritability fallacy |url=https://pzacad.pitzer.edu/~dmoore/publications/2016_moore--shenk_the-herit.pdf |journal=WIREs Cognitive Science |language=en |volume=8 |issue=1–2 |article-number=e1400 |doi=10.1002/wcs.1400 |pmid=27906501 |issn=1939-5078}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Tabery |first=James |url=https://mitpress.mit.edu/9780262549608/beyond-versus/ |title=Beyond Versus: The Struggle to Understand the Interaction of Nature and Nurture |date=31 October 2023 |publisher=The MIT Press |isbn=978-0-262-54960-8 |language=en-US}}</ref> They highlight their belief that heritability analysis requires a hidden assumption they call the "separation of causes", which isn't borne out by biological reality or experimental research.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Wahlsten |first=Douglas |date=July 1994 |title=The intelligence of heritability. |url=https://doi.apa.org/doi/10.1037/0708-5591.35.3.244 |journal=Canadian Psychology / Psychologie Canadienne |language=en |volume=35 |issue=3 |pages=244–260 |doi=10.1037/0708-5591.35.3.244 |issn=1878-7304|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Such researchers argue that the notion of heritability gives the false impression that "genes have some direct and isolated influence on traits", rather than another developmental resource that a complex system uses over the course of ontogeny.<ref name=":18" />

=== Between-group heritability ===
{{Main|Race and intelligence}}

Although IQ differences between individuals have been shown to have a hereditary component, it does not follow that differences in average IQ test performance between [[Race (human categorization)|racial]] and [[Ethnicity|ethnic]] groups have a genetic basis.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":1"/><ref name=":02"/> The scientific consensus is that genetics does not explain average differences in IQ test performance between racial groups.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal |last1=Ceci |first1=Stephen |last2=Williams |first2=Wendy M. |date=1 February 2009 |title=Should scientists study race and IQ? YES: The scientific truth must be pursued |journal=Nature |volume=457 |issue=7231 |pages=788–789 |bibcode=2009Natur.457..788C |doi=10.1038/457788a |pmid=19212385 |s2cid=205044224 |quote=There is an emerging consensus about racial and gender equality in genetic determinants of intelligence; most researchers, including ourselves, agree that genes do not explain between-group differences. |doi-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":6">{{Cite book |last=Hunt |first=Earl |url=https://archive.org/details/humanintelligenc0000hunt_s6m1/page/447/mode/1up?view=theater |title=Human Intelligence |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2010 |isbn=978-0-521-70781-7 |page=447 |ol=24384631M |quote=[N]o genes related to the difference in cognitive skills across the various racial and ethic groups have ever been discovered. |via=[[Open Library]] |ol-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":7">{{Cite book |last=Mackintosh, N. J. |url=https://archive.org/details/iqhumanintellige0000mack/mode/2up?view=theater |title=IQ and human intelligence |date=2011 |publisher=Oxford University Press |isbn=978-0-19-958559-5 |edition=2nd |location=Oxford |pages=334–338, 344 |oclc=669754008 |ol=25211083M |via=[[Open Library]] |ol-access=free}}</ref><ref name=":02"/><ref name=":5">{{Cite journal |last=Kaplan |first=Jonathan Michael |date=January 2015 |title=Race, IQ, and the search for statistical signals associated with so-called "X"-factors: environments, racism, and the "hereditarian hypothesis" |journal=Biology & Philosophy |language=en |volume=30 |issue=1 |pages=1–17 |doi=10.1007/s10539-014-9428-0 |issn=0169-3867 |s2cid=85351431}}</ref> Growing evidence indicates that environmental factors, not genetic ones, explain the racial IQ gap.<ref name=":02"/><ref name=":5" />{{sfn|Nevid|2014|page=271}}

Arguments in support of a genetic explanation of racial differences in average IQ are sometimes fallacious. For instance, some hereditarians have cited as evidence the failure of known environmental factors to account for such differences, or the high heritability of intelligence within races.<ref name=":9">{{Cite journal|last=Mackenzie|first=Brian|date=1984|title=Explaining race differences in IQ: The logic, the methodology, and the evidence|url=https://content.apa.org/record/1985-25462-001|journal=American Psychologist|volume=39|issue=11|pages=1214–1233|doi=10.1037/0003-066X.39.11.1214|via=|access-date=2021-01-29|archive-date=2021-02-02|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210202100805/https://content.apa.org/record/1985-25462-001|url-status=live}}</ref> In 1972, John DeFries attempted to connect "between group heritability" or ''h{{Sup|2}}''{{Sub|''B''}}  to "within group heritability" or ''h{{Sup|2}}''{{Sub|''W''}} in an equation <math>h^2_B\approx h^2_W \frac{(1-t)r}{(1-r)t}</math>, where ''r'' is the [[Intraclass correlation|intraclass]] genetic correlation among members of the same group, ''t'' is corresponding phenotypic intraclass correlation.<ref name=":8">{{Cite journal |last1=Schraiber |first1=Joshua G. |last2=Edge |first2=Michael D. |date=2024-03-19 |title=Heritability within groups is uninformative about differences among groups: Cases from behavioral, evolutionary, and statistical genetics |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America |volume=121 |issue=12 |article-number=e2319496121 |doi=10.1073/pnas.2319496121 |doi-access=free |issn=1091-6490 |pmc=10962975 |pmid=38470926 |bibcode=2024PNAS..12119496S }}</ref> However, this equation is tautological as the term ''r'' is defined in reference to variance among and between groups, meaning r, if anything, depends on ''h{{Sup|2}}''{{Sub|''B''}}.<ref name=":9" /><ref name=":8" /><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Feldman |first1=M. W. |last2=Lewontin |first2=R. C. |date=1975-12-19 |title=The heritability hang-up |journal=Science  |volume=190 |issue=4220 |pages=1163–1168 |doi=10.1126/science.1198102 |issn=0036-8075 |pmid=1198102 |bibcode=1975Sci...190.1163F }}</ref> Geneticists Joshua Schraiber and Michael Edge showed that even if this quantity r is known, the quantity ''h{{Sup|2}}''{{Sub|''B''}} is still consistent with "infinitely many configurations of genetic differences among populations".<ref name=":8" /> They conclude:<blockquote>Perfect knowledge of within-group heritability provides no information about between-group heritability. Crucially, even if the heritability of between-group differences is estimated correctly, it leaves the direction of the genetic and environmental components of phenotypic difference unclear.</blockquote>In 2017, the editorial board of ''[[Nature (journal)|Nature]]'' to issued a statement differentiating current research on the genetics of intelligence from the [[Scientific racism|racist pseudoscience]] which it acknowledged has dogged intelligence research since its inception.<ref name="Nature-2017">{{Cite journal |date=25 May 2017 |title=Intelligence research should not be held back by its past |journal=Nature |volume=545 |issue=7655 |pages=385–386 |bibcode=2017Natur.545R.385. |doi=10.1038/nature.2017.22021 |pmid=28541341 |s2cid=4449918 |doi-access=free}}</ref> It characterized the idea of genetically determined differences in intelligence between races as definitively false.<ref name="Nature-2017" /> Analysis of polygenic scores sampled from the [[1000 Genomes Project]] has likewise found no evidence that intelligence was under diversifying selection in Africans and Europeans, suggesting that genetic differences cannot be a significant factor in the observed Black-White gap in average IQ test performance.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bird |first=Kevin A. |date=2 February 2021 |title=No support for the hereditarian hypothesis of the Black–White achievement gap using polygenic scores and tests for divergent selection |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.1002/ajpa.24216 |journal=[[American Journal of Physical Anthropology]] |language=en |volume=175 |issue=2 |pages=465–476 |bibcode=2021AJPA..175..465B |doi=10.1002/ajpa.24216 |issn=0002-9483 |pmid=33529393 |url-access=subscription |access-date=1 November 2024 |via=Wiley Online Library}}</ref>
